segments.text: How did a fabric woven in China end up in the wardrobes of Roman senators, six thousand kilometers away?
Starting around one hundred thirty BC, under the Han dynasty, traders began linking China to the Mediterranean. It was never one road, but a web of routes across deserts and mountains.
Here is the main route, from Chang'an in China, through Central Asia and Persia, to the ports of the Mediterranean.
Almost nobody traveled the whole way. Goods passed hand to hand, through merchant after merchant, and each one took a cut.
Silk was the star, but spices, paper, glass, horses and precious metals moved too.
Ideas rode along with the caravans. Buddhism spread from India into China, paper and printing moved west, and so did gunpowder and the compass.
Trade also carried danger. In the thirteen forties, the Black Death likely spread along these same routes and reached Europe in thirteen forty-seven.
The routes faded after the fourteen hundreds, as Ottoman control grew and ships opened sea routes around Africa and across the oceans.
So that Roman silk? It passed through dozens of hands over thousands of kilometers. The Silk Road was a chain of exchange, and it connected the world long before the modern age.
